overview.text: Skiing is travel and sport on snow using skis, long pieces of equipment attached to the feet. Archaeological finds and rock art show that skis were used in northern Europe thousands of years ago, especially as practical tools for getting around; the evidence does not establish one simple birthplace. Over time, different ski designs and styles developed for varied terrain and activities. Modern skiing includes several distinct competitive branches, such as alpine skiing, cross-country, ski jumping, Nordic combined and freestyle—not only downhill skiing at resorts. The International Ski and Snowboard Federation, founded in 1924, governs major international disciplines and sets competition rules. Skiing’s significance reflects its transformation from winter transport into recreation and organized sport.

key_facts.text: Ski use in northern Europe dates back thousands of years: rock art and preserved skis provide evidence, though they do not prove where skiing first began.
Skis were practical equipment for winter travel, hunting and communication before skiing became a widespread sport and recreation.
Ski designs differ by activity; alpine and cross-country skis, for example, are among several specialized types.
FIS recognizes branches including alpine skiing, cross-country, ski jumping, Nordic combined and freestyle skiing, and sets international competition rules.
The Ski Museum at Holmenkollen, established in 1923, describes its collection as presenting 5,000 years of skiing history.
